newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan racketeer payoff scandal threatens to widen.
newsitem.headline: Japan racketeer payoff scandal threatens to widen.

text.p: Japan's high-profile racketeer payoff scandal threatened to widen on Monday after the corporate extortionist at the heart of the affair reportedly confessed to illegal deals with three more big brokerages.

The scandal has already led to more than a dozen arrests of officials from Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB), one of Japan's biggest banks, and giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd, and to the suicide on Sunday of a senior DKB banker.

On Monday, domestic media said "sokaiya" racketeer Ryuichi Koike had told prosecutors that Nikko Securities Co Ltd, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd and Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd all carried out deals on his behalf through illegal discretionary accounts.
Spokesmen for the three brokerages declined comment.

On Friday, Nikko president Kichiro Takao told an annual shareholders' meeting that he was not aware of any illegal payments by the brokerage to shareholders. And Yamaichi president Atsuo Miki also denied at Friday's shareholders' gathering that the brokerage had done any illegal deals.

Industry experts have speculated that other firms could be ensnared in a manner reminiscent of the 1991 financial scandals that forced Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, then finance minister, to hand in his finance portfolio.

An opposition lawmaker earlier this month made public documents from DKB indicating that in the seven years to March 1996, 17 brokerages transferred a total of 1.72 billion yen ($15.0 million) to accounts held at the bank by Ryuichi Koike's younger brother.
The documents showed Nikko had transferred 1.1 billion yen ($9.6 million), the biggest amount among the 17 brokerages.
On Sunday, meanwhile, a former top DKB official seen as a key figure in prosecutors' probe of the scandal committed suicide, casting a cloud over the investigation.

Former Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB) chairman Kuniji Miyazaki, 67, died in hospital on Sunday after hanging himself at his home following questioning by prosecutors over his role in the payoff scandal involving "sokaiya" corporate extortionists.
The scandal has emerged just as Japan kicks off "Big Bang" financial reforms that experts say make a corporate ethics clean-up and improved official surveillance vital.
Authorities -- including Hashimoto -- have taken a tough public stance towards the latest corporate misdeeds, which they fear could cast doubt on the credibility of planned reforms.

"As a public official, I think that if he (Miyazaki) really had the courage to choose the course of death, I wanted him to demonstrate his courage to reveal the truth," Hashimoto told reporters on Monday.

A prominent figure in financial circles who had been expected to become a member of the Bank of Japan's policy board before the scandal broke, Miyazaki stepped down as DKB adviser in mid-June after acknowledging contacts with the racketeer.

Some analysts had said the suicide might dampen public enthusiasm for a further probe, but the fresh reports of other brokerages' involvement could deprive authorities of the option of limiting the lesson in corporate ethics to Nomura and DKB.

"They (the Finance Ministry) have been remarkably good about looking in the wrong places so far despite evidence suggesting others had dealings with Koike," said David Threadgold, financial analyst at BZW Securities. "But if Koike is spilling his guts, it's going to be hard to look the other way."

Payoffs to sokaiya, who typically extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholders' meetings or otherwise expose corporate misdeeds, have been illegal since 1983. But many firms have found it hard to halt the practice.
